Emma — thanks for the clear questions. I pulled this together with help from our pricing and runtime teams. I attached the Q2 rate card and a CSV with worked examples; below are concise rules and a few numeric examples you can drop into a model.

Short answers up front:
- Yes: system messages are billed and treated as input tokens.
- Tool/function outputs are billed as output tokens. If you take tool output and send it back as input in a subsequent request, those tokens will also be billed as input at that later request.
- Billing is token-accurate (based on our tokenizer) and we bill at per-token granularity; we express prices per 1,000 tokens on the rate card but compute charges from exact token counts (no forced 1K rounding-up).
- Streaming: tokens are billed as they are produced, but the underlying accounting uses the tokenizer-imputed counts; partial/byte-level fragments are rounded up to the next whole tokenizer token.

Examples (using the exact tokenizer counts produced by our runtime):

Example A — simple chat turn
- System prompt: 180 tokens (counts as input)
- User message: 40 tokens (input)
- Model response streamed: 480 tokens (output)
- Total billed: input = 220 tokens, output = 480 tokens. We compute cost = (220 * input_rate) + (480 * output_rate).

Example B — function/tool flow
- User asks to fetch docs (20 tokens input)
- Model emits function call (the function name + args JSON) — tokenizer says 36 tokens; that function call is part of the model's output (so billed as output).
- Your retrieval service returns 1,200 tokens as tool output. When the runtime injects that retrieval text into the model as a new request (context), those 1,200 tokens are billed as input for that new request.
- If you then get a follow-up model answer of 320 tokens, that 320 is billed as output.
- Summary billing for the end-to-end interaction: output tokens = 36 (function call) + 320 (final answer) = 356; input tokens = 20 (user) + 1,200 (retrieval fed back in) = 1,220.

Important nuance: we do NOT double-bill the same bytes in the same model call. Example: function call arguments that the model produced are output tokens; if you immediately echo those same bytes back into the same running request (unlikely), our runtime still counts them once. The common double-counting happens when a tool executes outside the model and you later feed that tool output into a new model request — that is separate input billing.

Rounding specifics:
- Tokenization rounding: any fractional tokenizer unit is rounded up to the next token prior to billing.
- Aggregation/invoice: we show rates as $/1K tokens, but the invoice is calculated from summed token counts across the billing period; we do not round every request up to 1K before summing. Example: two requests of 600 tokens and 600 tokens total 1,200 tokens and are billed for 1,200, not 2,000.

Great questions — answered inline below, with another worked example showing timing and streaming.

1) Tool outputs and streaming: the runtime bills tokens when they are produced by the component that emits them. Practically this means:
   - If the model emits a function call (output) that contains arguments, those argument bytes are billed as output.
   - If your external retrieval tool emits text (the retrieval service returns rows) and we proxy that as "tool output" back to the client without injecting it into the model, those bytes are billed as tool/output tokens but only on the tool side (i.e., they appear as outbound bytes from our tool adapter). They become billed input tokens only when we create a subsequent model request that includes them in the context.
   - We do not double-bill the exact same bytes in a single request. Double counting only occurs across distinct requests where the same data crosses the model boundary twice (once as tool output, once as model input).

Streaming nuance example (timing):
- T0: User sends prompt (30 tokens). Model emits function call (40 tokens) — billed as output = 40.
- T1: Client receives function call and concurrently calls your retrieval service. Retrieval returns 1,100 tokens and we stream that back to the client as tool output — billed as tool/output = 1,100. At this stage the model has not yet seen the retrieval text, so model input = 30 only.
- T2: Client asks model to continue and includes the retrieval text in a new request; that new request has input = 1,100 (retrieval) + 30 (user context) = 1,130 and the model returns answer = 400 (output).
- Billing summary: first request: input 30 / output 40; tool output (proxy) 1,100; second request: input 1,130 / output 400. Invoice shows all of those tokens, with the retrieval tokens appearing first as tool output and then as input when they are fed back into the model — so you see them twice across the end-to-end flow, which is correct because there were two separate billable operations.

2) Dedicated (Reserved capacity): token accounting rules are identical. The differences are pricing structure (you get lower per-1K rates per your committed tier) and quotas/throughput guarantees. We do not change what counts as input/output on Dedicated. We can, however, grant more verbose debugging traces for your engineering team during the PoC so you can reconcile counts automatically.

3) Splitting function args: billing is based on the bytes emitted by the model and later used. If you keep the initial function arguments minimal (cheap) and only inject large payloads later as separate requests, you will shift billing from the initial output to later input (the economic outcome is the same in total tokens, but timing and whether something is counted as output vs input will differ). That can matter for quota windows or for tracing but not for total token math.
